common_name: Red-Lid Yellow Trumpet Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia Flava Var. Atropurpurea)

planting.note: Divide and replant rhizome sections into pure sphagnum moss or a 1:1 peat-sand carnivorous plant mix in full sun, watering only with distilled or rain water; this variety is identified by its solid deep maroon-red lid contrasting against an otherwise unmarked chartreuse-yellow pitcher.

directions: Divide and replant rhizome sections into pure sphagnum moss or a 1:1 peat-sand carnivorous plant mix in full sun, watering only with distilled or rain water; this variety is identified by its solid deep maroon-red lid contrasting against an otherwise unmarked chartreuse-yellow pitcher. Tall, trumpet-shaped pitchers form in early spring alongside nodding yellow flowers before the true pitchers fully open, luring flying insects with sweet nectar drooled along the throat. This dark-lidded form occurs scattered through the same Gulf Coast pine savanna bogs as ordinary flava and is prized by collectors for the strong color contrast on an otherwise pale plant. Give it a cool, bright winter dormancy with reduced watering to trigger reliable flowering the following season.
sources: Atlanta Botanical Garden Carnivorous Plant Collection

common_name: Giant Unmarked Yellow Trumpet Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia Flava Var. Maxima)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes and set into pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in full sun, watering only with distilled or rain water; this form lacks any red veining or throat blotch found on typical flava, giving a clean, entirely green-gold pitcher.

directions: Divide rhizomes and set into pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in full sun, watering only with distilled or rain water; this form lacks any red veining or throat blotch found on typical flava, giving a clean, entirely green-gold pitcher. It is among the most vigorous and largest-growing of all flava varieties, with mature clumps sending up an impressive stand of erect trumpets each spring. The unmarked lid and tube make it stand out sharply next to the copper-topped and red-throated forms of the same species when grown side by side. Provide a cool, bright winter rest with minimal watering, then resume heavy watering as new pitchers emerge in spring.

common_name: Alabama Canebrake Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia Rubra Subsp. Alabamensis)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes into pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in full to partial sun, watering only with distilled or rain water; this subspecies survives today at only a handful of protected central Alabama seepage bog sites and is federally listed as endangered.

directions: Divide rhizomes into pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in full to partial sun, watering only with distilled or rain water; this subspecies survives today at only a handful of protected central Alabama seepage bog sites and is federally listed as endangered. Slender maroon-red pitchers rise from canebrake understory habitat, historically growing in the light shade of native river cane rather than fully open bog. Nodding, sweetly fragrant maroon flowers open in mid-spring before the new season's pitchers fully unfurl. Cultivated stock in collections and botanical gardens plays an important role in conservation, so plants of documented, ethically propagated origin should always be chosen.
sources: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service Species Profile

common_name: Gulf Coast Sweet Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia Rubra Subsp. Gulfensis)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes into pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in full sun, watering only with distilled or rain water; native to Florida Panhandle and coastal Alabama bogs, this is the tallest and most robust of the sweet pitcher plant subspecies.

directions: Divide rhizomes into pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in full sun, watering only with distilled or rain water; native to Florida Panhandle and coastal Alabama bogs, this is the tallest and most robust of the sweet pitcher plant subspecies. Narrow, upright reddish-veined pitchers cluster into dense colonies far larger than the typical inland rubra, and the plant tolerates the humid, mild-winter Gulf climate especially well. Deep maroon, sweetly scented flowers nod above the foliage in spring on wiry stalks. Keep the crown constantly wet through the growing season and allow only a brief, mild winter rest.

common_name: Wherry's Sweet Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia Rubra Subsp. Wherryi)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes into pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in full sun, watering only with distilled or rain water; named for botanist Edgar Wherry, this Alabama-Mississippi subspecies is distinguished from typical rubra by its more erect, rounder hood.

directions: Divide rhizomes into pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in full sun, watering only with distilled or rain water; named for botanist Edgar Wherry, this Alabama-Mississippi subspecies is distinguished from typical rubra by its more erect, rounder hood. Slender maroon pitchers form compact clumps smaller than the Gulf Coast form, well suited to container bog gardens. Spring flowers are deep red-maroon and carry a light, sweet fragrance that draws pollinating flies and beetles. As with all sweet pitcher plants, a distinct cool winter dormancy with reduced watering keeps the rhizome healthy for years.

common_name: Chelson's Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia x Chelsonii, Purpurea-Rubra Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes into pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in full sun, watering only with distilled or rain water; this natural and long-cultivated hybrid between Sarracenia purpurea and Sarracenia rubra was among the first pitcher plant crosses grown in Victorian-era European glasshouses.

directions: Divide rhizomes into pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in full sun, watering only with distilled or rain water; this natural and long-cultivated hybrid between Sarracenia purpurea and Sarracenia rubra was among the first pitcher plant crosses grown in Victorian-era European glasshouses. Pitchers are intermediate in form between the two parents, more upright than purpurea's squat tubes but flushed with the same reddish-purple veining, and the hybrid shows noticeable vigor over either species alone. It occurs spontaneously in the wild wherever the ranges of purpurea and rubra overlap in the Carolinas. Give it the same cold winter dormancy purpurea requires, since this parentage keeps it considerably hardier than most red-flowered Sarracenia hybrids.

planting.note: Root leaf cuttings or set young divisions into a 1:1 peat-sand mix or pure sphagnum moss kept in a tray of distilled or rain water in full sun; leaves overlap tightly around the crown in a spiral that resembles a small woven bird's nest.

directions: Root leaf cuttings or set young divisions into a 1:1 peat-sand mix or pure sphagnum moss kept in a tray of distilled or rain water in full sun; leaves overlap tightly around the crown in a spiral that resembles a small woven bird's nest. This South African rosette sundew is closely related to the more common Cape sundew and Alice sundew but stays noticeably more compact and dense. Fine reddish tentacles cover each wedge-shaped leaf and curl inward within an hour of catching a gnat or fruit fly. It tolerates warmer, more humid conditions than most temperate sundews, making it an easy candidate for a sunny windowsill bog tray or greenhouse bench.

planting.note: Root leaf cuttings or set divisions into pure sphagnum moss or a peat-sand carnivorous plant mix kept standing in distilled or rain water in full sun; this Western Cape species forms a larger, flatter rosette than its close relative Drosera aliciae.

directions: Root leaf cuttings or set divisions into pure sphagnum moss or a peat-sand carnivorous plant mix kept standing in distilled or rain water in full sun; this Western Cape species forms a larger, flatter rosette than its close relative Drosera aliciae. Broad, spoon-shaped leaves are densely fringed with long reddish tentacles that glisten heavily with sticky dew, giving the whole plant a jewel-like appearance in bright light. Showy pink-and-white flowers rise on tall stalks well above the foliage and open readily on sunny mornings. Its tolerance for a wide range of humidity and light levels makes it one of the more forgiving rosetted sundews for beginning growers.

planting.note: Surface-sow fine seed onto damp peat-sand or milled sphagnum in autumn and keep constantly wet in bright, cool conditions; this Australian annual grows through the mild winter and dies back completely once summer heat and drought arrive.

directions: Surface-sow fine seed onto damp peat-sand or milled sphagnum in autumn and keep constantly wet in bright, cool conditions; this Australian annual grows through the mild winter and dies back completely once summer heat and drought arrive. It is famous among carnivorous plant enthusiasts for its outer 'snap tentacles,' which flick unsuspecting insects toward the sticky central leaf surface within a fraction of a second, among the fastest movements recorded in any sundew. A tiny flat rosette hugs the ground while a slender, leafless flower stalk rises above it to display small orange-centered white flowers. Because it self-sows readily, established pots often replenish themselves each season if seed is allowed to scatter into the growing medium.

planting.note: Separate rooted plantlets and pot into pure sphagnum moss or a peat-sand mix kept constantly moist in a warm, shaded terrarium rather than direct sun, unlike most sun-loving sundews.

directions: Separate rooted plantlets and pot into pure sphagnum moss or a peat-sand mix kept constantly moist in a warm, shaded terrarium rather than direct sun, unlike most sun-loving sundews. Native to the dim rainforest floor of tropical Queensland, this small sundew produces slender flowering stalks that sprout tiny new plantlets along their length, which root wherever they touch damp moss to form new colonies. Round leaves are covered in short, glistening tentacles adapted to catching small fungus gnats in low light rather than bright, open bog conditions. High humidity and warm year-round temperatures are essential, so it is best suited to a covered terrarium rather than an outdoor bog tray.

planting.note: Plant dormant pea-sized tubers 2-3 inches deep in a sandy peat mix in autumn and keep evenly moist through the cool growing season, then withhold water completely and let the pot dry out once foliage yellows for summer dormancy.

directions: Plant dormant pea-sized tubers 2-3 inches deep in a sandy peat mix in autumn and keep evenly moist through the cool growing season, then withhold water completely and let the pot dry out once foliage yellows for summer dormancy. Unlike the rosetted sundews familiar to most growers, this Australian and Asian species sends up a thin, scrambling stem lined with small round, shield-shaped (peltate) sticky leaves that can lean on nearby plants for support. It flowers with delicate white to pink blooms atop the stem before dying back completely to the underground tuber each dry season. Because it needs a genuine dry dormancy to reset the tuber, resist watering the pot at all during its rest period even though this feels counterintuitive for a carnivorous plant.

planting.note: Surface-sow fine seed onto wet peat-sand or milled sphagnum under a humidity dome and keep hot and constantly saturated; move to an outdoor bog tray only once nights stay reliably above 65F.

directions: Surface-sow fine seed onto wet peat-sand or milled sphagnum under a humidity dome and keep hot and constantly saturated; move to an outdoor bog tray only once nights stay reliably above 65F. This pantropical sundew, native across Africa, Asia, and Australia, grows as an erect warm-season annual with thin, thread-like leaves densely covered in sticky red tentacles that ensnare small flying insects. Delicate pink flowers open in succession up the stem through the hottest part of summer. Give it full sun, very high humidity, and hot growing conditions, since it has no cold tolerance and will die with the first cool night of autumn.

planting.note: Propagate from leaf pullings and pot into a mineral Mexican-Pinguicula mix of equal parts sand, perlite, and peat, watering with distilled or rain water and letting the surface dry briefly between waterings unlike most bog carnivores.

directions: Propagate from leaf pullings and pot into a mineral Mexican-Pinguicula mix of equal parts sand, perlite, and peat, watering with distilled or rain water and letting the surface dry briefly between waterings unlike most bog carnivores. This popular hybrid butterwort is grown chiefly for its oversized lavender-pink flowers, which are held on tall stalks well above a broad rosette of sticky, flypaper-like summer leaves. In cooler months it contracts into a tight, non-carnivorous succulent winter rosette and needs much less water until new sticky leaves resume in spring. Its ease of care and showy blooms have made it a favorite beginner butterwort widely offered by carnivorous plant nurseries.

planting.note: Propagate from leaf pullings into a mineral mix of sand, perlite, and peat, watering with distilled or rain water and allowing the surface to dry slightly between waterings during the succulent winter rosette stage.

directions: Propagate from leaf pullings into a mineral mix of sand, perlite, and peat, watering with distilled or rain water and allowing the surface to dry slightly between waterings during the succulent winter rosette stage. Native to limestone cliffs and seepage areas in northeastern Mexico, this species bears pale creamy-white to yellow-green flowers, an unusual color among Pinguicula that mostly bloom pink or purple. Broad, pale-green summer leaves are covered in a fine glistening mucilage that traps gnats and fungus flies. Several natural color forms are grown in cultivation, all sharing the same easy windowsill culture that has made it a common entry point into growing Mexican butterworts.

planting.note: Propagate from leaf pullings into a mineral mix of sand, perlite, and peat, watering with distilled or rain water and reducing water sharply once the plant switches into its narrow winter leaf form.

directions: Propagate from leaf pullings into a mineral mix of sand, perlite, and peat, watering with distilled or rain water and reducing water sharply once the plant switches into its narrow winter leaf form. Native to gypsum outcrops in Mexico, this species is unmatched among cultivated butterworts for its dramatic seasonal heterophylly: a flat, sticky, insect-catching rosette in the wet growing season gives way to slender, non-carnivorous cylindrical leaves that curl at the tips during the dry winter dormancy. Small pink flowers appear on thin stalks during the transition between the two leaf forms. Because the winter leaves photograph and grow so differently from the summer rosette, new growers sometimes mistake the plant for two different species in the same pot.

planting.note: Propagate from leaf pullings into a mineral mix of sand, perlite, and peat, watering with distilled or rain water and allowing brief surface drying between waterings as with other Mexican butterworts.

directions: Propagate from leaf pullings into a mineral mix of sand, perlite, and peat, watering with distilled or rain water and allowing brief surface drying between waterings as with other Mexican butterworts. Native to cloud forest habitat in Oaxaca, Mexico, this species is prized for its vivid magenta-red flowers, an unusually saturated color among Pinguicula, most of which bloom in softer pinks, purples, or white. A moderate-sized rosette of sticky, yellow-green summer leaves traps gnats and small flies with a coating of glistening mucilage. High humidity and bright, indirect light bring out the strongest flower color and the healthiest leaf growth.

planting.note: Plant fine rhizome sections into a nutrient-poor bog mix or aquarium substrate kept fully saturated or shallowly submersed under bright light, ideally with CO2 supplementation for aquascaping use; small purple flowers form only when leaves are grown emersed above the waterline.

directions: Plant fine rhizome sections into a nutrient-poor bog mix or aquarium substrate kept fully saturated or shallowly submersed under bright light, ideally with CO2 supplementation for aquascaping use; small purple flowers form only when leaves are grown emersed above the waterline. Native to shallow wet meadows and rice paddy margins across Southeast Asia, its fine, grass-like leaves form a low, spreading carpet valued by planted-aquarium hobbyists as a foreground groundcover. Underwater it functions like any other bladderwort, deploying microscopic bladder traps along its rhizomes to capture tiny aquatic organisms for nutrition. Regular trimming keeps the carpet dense and prevents it from climbing toward the surface in high-light tanks.

planting.note: Scatter a pinch of fine rhizome and seed material over pure sphagnum moss or a peat-sand mix kept in a tray of distilled or rain water in full sun; this easy terrestrial bladderwort self-sows and fills in a pot quickly.

directions: Scatter a pinch of fine rhizome and seed material over pure sphagnum moss or a peat-sand mix kept in a tray of distilled or rain water in full sun; this easy terrestrial bladderwort self-sows and fills in a pot quickly. Native to seasonally wet flats in South Africa, its threadlike underground stems bear tiny bladder traps that capture soil-dwelling microorganisms and protozoa. Abundant small white-and-yellow or purple snapdragon-like flowers appear almost continuously through the warm growing season, making it unusually showy for such a diminutive carnivorous plant. Its tolerance for a wide range of conditions and rapid spread make it one of the most forgiving terrestrial bladderworts for beginners.

planting.note: Mount divisions on wet sphagnum moss or pot into a fine peat-sand mix kept permanently saturated with distilled or rain water in bright, humid, partially shaded conditions typical of its epiphytic Brazilian mountain habitat.

directions: Mount divisions on wet sphagnum moss or pot into a fine peat-sand mix kept permanently saturated with distilled or rain water in bright, humid, partially shaded conditions typical of its epiphytic Brazilian mountain habitat. This striking bladderwort produces unusually large, kidney-shaped leaves among the biggest found anywhere in the genus, growing terrestrially or perched on wet rock faces and mossy tree trunks. From these leaves it sends up tall, wiry flower spikes bearing large violet-purple blooms resembling small orchids. Because of its impressive foliage and flowers, it is one of the most sought-after collector's Utricularia in cultivation, though it needs consistently high humidity to thrive.

planting.note: Introduce free-floating stems directly into a sunny outdoor pond, water garden, or tub without soil or anchoring; use rain or untreated pond water rather than chlorinated tap water, as this rootless plant draws nutrients only from captured prey and the water itself.

directions: Introduce free-floating stems directly into a sunny outdoor pond, water garden, or tub without soil or anchoring; use rain or untreated pond water rather than chlorinated tap water, as this rootless plant draws nutrients only from captured prey and the water itself. Widespread across temperate ponds, ditches, and slow streams of North America, Europe, and Asia, it forms large submerged mats of finely divided leaves studded with thousands of tiny bladder traps that snap shut in milliseconds to capture water fleas and other small invertebrates. Bright yellow, snapdragon-like flowers rise a few inches above the water surface on slender stalks through summer. In autumn it produces dense, compact winter buds called turions that sink to the pond bottom and resume growth automatically the following spring, making it one of the hardiest and lowest-maintenance carnivorous plants for an outdoor water garden.
